section.title: The Commander of the LORD's Army
section.sectionRationale: On the eve of Jericho, Joshua meets a mysterious armed man and asks the natural question of a general: whose side are you on? The answer redraws everything. This is not an ally who has come to take Israel's side, but the Commander of the LORD's army who has come to take command, and the ground turns holy under Joshua's feet. It is one brief but pivotal movement, the encounter that reveals who truly leads the conquest.
section.thesis: The battle for the land is not Israel's war that God will assist, but the LORD's war that Israel is summoned to join; so the true Commander appears, sword drawn, and calls Joshua not to recruit Him but to bow, worship, and take his orders on holy ground.
section.frameNote: One movement in three quick exchanges: Joshua's challenge to the armed man, verse 13; the Commander's answer and Joshua's worship, verse 14; and the command to remove his sandals on holy ground, verse 15.

units.label: The armed man before Jericho
units.note: are You for us or for our enemies

verses.text: Now when Joshua was near Jericho, he looked up and saw a man standing in front of him with a drawn sword in His hand. Joshua approached Him and asked, “Are You for us or for our enemies?”

units.label: The Commander's answer and Joshua's worship
units.note: I have come as Commander of the LORD's army

verses.text: “Neither,” He replied. “I have now come as Commander of the LORD’s {{tsava|army}}.” Then Joshua fell facedown in {{shachah|reverence}} and asked Him, “What does my Lord have to say to His servant?”

units.label: Holy ground
units.note: take off your sandals, for this place is holy

verses.text: The Commander of the LORD’s army replied, “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is {{qodesh|holy}}.” And Joshua did so.

tsava.gloss: Army, host, company arrayed for war. The figure is Commander of the tsava of the LORD, the host of heaven. The title recalls the LORD of hosts, the God who leads uncountable armies; it declares that the real force behind the conquest is heavenly, and that Joshua's men are joining a war the LORD is already waging.

shachah.gloss: To bow down, prostrate oneself, worship. Joshua falls facedown before the Commander, an act of worship that the figure receives, unlike the holy angel in Revelation 22:8-9 who refuses it. That He accepts worship, and calls the ground holy, marks Him out as more than a created angel, an appearance of the LORD Himself.

qodesh.gloss: Holiness, that which is set apart because God is present. The ground is holy not by nature but because the LORD stands there, exactly as at the burning bush, Exodus 3:5. The command to remove the sandals binds this scene to Moses' call and confirms that Joshua stands in the presence of the holy God who commissions and leads His people.

basic.context: Joshua is scouting near Jericho when he suddenly sees a man standing before him with a drawn sword. Like any commander, Joshua challenges him: are you on our side or the enemy's? The answer is startling: Neither. I have come as Commander of the LORD's army. This is not a soldier choosing sides in Israel's war; this is the LORD's own Commander come to take charge of His war. Joshua immediately falls facedown and worships, asking for orders, and is told to remove his sandals because the ground is holy, the same words spoken to Moses at the burning bush. The question underneath is: whose battle is the conquest, really, and who is in command?
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative, and the brief scene is heavy with theological weight. The figure receives worship and calls the ground holy, which a mere creature would refuse, so the church has long understood this as a christophany, an appearance of the pre-incarnate Son, or at least of the LORD Himself. The passage does not give battle tactics; it resets Joshua's whole frame of reference, teaching that God does not join our causes so much as call us into His.
basic.originalLanguages: The figure is Commander of the tsava, the army or host, of the LORD, the heavenly force behind the conquest. Joshua falls in shachah, worship, which the Commander accepts. And the ground is qodesh, holy, because the LORD is present, echoing Moses at the burning bush.
basic.typology: The Commander who leads the LORD's heavenly army points to Christ, the captain of our salvation who leads His people to victory, and who appears in Revelation with the armies of heaven. The holy ground and the removed sandals bind Joshua's commissioning to Moses', both standing before the same holy LORD.
basic.christ: Many understand this armed Commander who receives worship to be the pre-incarnate Christ, the same LORD who appeared to Moses. Whether or not one presses that identification, the scene reveals the true Captain of the LORD's hosts, and the New Testament names Jesus the pioneer and captain of our salvation, Hebrews 2:10, and shows Him leading the armies of heaven, Revelation 19:11-14.
basic.god: God reveals Himself as the true Commander of the conquest. He is holy, turning ordinary ground holy by His presence. He is sovereign, not a partisan ally to be recruited but the Lord of hosts who summons Joshua to His side. The right posture before Him is not negotiation but worship and glad obedience.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 3 records the burning bush, where Moses is told to remove his sandals on holy ground. Revelation 19 shows Christ leading the armies of heaven. Hebrews 2 calls Jesus the captain of our salvation. And Revelation 22 shows a holy angel refusing the worship this Commander accepts.
basic.oneStory: Before Jericho falls, the LORD reveals that the conquest is His war, led by His Commander, and Joshua must worship rather than recruit Him. The scene points to Christ, the true Captain of the LORD's hosts, who leads His people in the real battle and before whom every knee will bow.

context.literary:
This scene forms the quiet capstone of chapter 5, following two rites that renew the covenant community on the very eve of war: the flint knife circumcision of a generation born in the wilderness, and the first Passover kept in the land, after which the manna stops for good, verses 2 to 12. Three thresholds in a row, circumcision, Passover, and now this meeting, prepare Joshua's men before a sword is lifted in Canaan. The narrator gives almost nothing away. There is no description of the setting beyond near Jericho, no build up, only a bare report: a man, a drawn sword, three short exchanges, and the scene ends as abruptly as it began, the text moving straight on to Jericho's shut gates in 6:1 without so much as a note that Joshua walked away. That economy is deliberate; the encounter exists to reframe everything that follows, not to be savored as a story in its own right.

The withheld identity drives the plot. The narrator calls Him only a man, and Joshua treats Him as a scout would treat any armed stranger, issuing a soldier's challenge. Only the reply forces a reassessment, and Joshua's own posture, falling facedown, becomes the reader's clue to who this is before the text ever states it plainly. This is also the second commissioning scene bracketing Israel's entry into the land: the LORD spoke directly to Joshua at the book's opening, 1:1 to 9, and now, at the threshold of the first battle, a still higher authority appears bodily, so the entry narrative opens and turns on two moments of divine address, one spoken, one seen.
context.historical:
A lone armed man on the approach to a besieged city gave no clue whose side he was on; ancient armies wore no uniforms to mark friend from foe, so Joshua's blunt question was the ordinary caution of any commander sizing up a stranger before a campaign. The title the figure claims, however, was not exotic. Sar, commander, was the everyday rank of a human general elsewhere in Israel's history, Sisera the commander of Jabin's forces at Hazor, Judges 4:2, and Abner the commander of Saul's army, 2 Samuel 2:8. Joshua had every reason at first to take the words at face value and expect an officer, friendly or hostile, not a theophany.

Falling facedown was likewise not, by itself, an act reserved for deity. It was the standard gesture of deference before any superior in that world; David bows facedown before Saul in a cave, 1 Samuel 24:8, and Mephibosheth falls facedown before David, 2 Samuel 9:6. What marks this encounter as more than diplomatic courtesy is not the bow but what follows it: the figure does not deflect the worship, as a mortal officer would, and He goes on to declare the very dust holy, a claim that belongs to God alone. Removing sandals in that world signified leaving behind the ordinary business of the road, exactly the gesture Moses had already been given at the very same kind of ground, generations earlier.
context.canonical:
The same picture, an armed messenger who meets a leader and receives immediate prostration, recurs three times in the historical books. Balaam's donkey sees before Balaam does, but once his eyes are opened he too finds the angel of the LORD standing in the road with a drawn sword, and falls facedown, Numbers 22:31. Centuries later David lifts up his eyes and sees the angel of the LORD standing between heaven and earth with a drawn sword, this time turned in judgment against Jerusalem, and again the response is to fall facedown, 1 Chronicles 21:16. Joshua's meeting is the first and gentlest of the three: the sword is drawn but never against Israel, and the message is an invitation into a war already being won, not a rebuke for one already lost.

Daniel later calls the angelic guardian of Israel Michael, the great prince, one of the chief princes, using the same word for rank that Joshua's Commander bears, Daniel 10:13,21 and 12:1, which is part of why some readers connect the two figures. Others hear in the title an anticipation of Isaiah's promise that God would give His servant to the nations as a leader and commander of the peoples, Isaiah 55:4, a line the church has long read as messianic. However the identification is drawn, the canon keeps returning to this same picture: an armed figure, a fallen leader, and a word from the LORD that reorders everything that follows.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses is the model the narrator keeps in view. By reproducing the burning bush's very words, take off your sandals, the author means his first hearers to recognize Joshua as Moses' true heir, commissioned by the same LORD in the same terms, not a lesser stand in leading a diminished campaign. The timing matters too: this is the last thing that happens before the assault on Jericho begins, so the author places it exactly where it will color everything that follows, seven days of marching in chapter 6, the disaster at Ai in chapter 7, the whole conquest. Readers are meant to carry this scene with them through every later battle report and remember that the fighting they read about next was never Israel's own to win or lose by its own resources.

The author also means to correct a natural but wrong instinct, treating God's help as something Israel possesses and can call on. Joshua's very question, betraying that instinct, gets answered by neither, forcing a change of posture from commander to servant within a single verse. Later hearers under kings tempted to treat the ark or the temple as guarantees of victory regardless of their own faithfulness needed exactly this correction: God leads; He is not led.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: Nothing in the passage instructs later readers to expect a literal, armed visitor before their own battles, and turning it into a search for comparable visions misses the point of a scene the author never repeats even later in his own book. What is meant to carry forward is a pattern of prayer: Joshua does not ask this figure for tactical advice or for reassurance that the outcome will go his way, he asks only what does my Lord have to say, and then obeys the single instruction he receives. That reordering of prayer, from petition that bends God to human plans toward a posture that waits for God's own word, applies whether or not anyone today ever meets an armed figure on a road. The chapter also warns against reading any success, spiritual or otherwise, as proof that God has joined a particular side; the text insists the reverse question is the right one to ask.

debates.question: Who is the Commander of the LORD's army?

views.label: A christophany, the pre-incarnate Son
views.case: The figure receives Joshua's worship and declares the ground holy, things a created angel refuses to do, Revelation 22:8-9; He speaks with divine authority and stands where the LORD stood before Moses, so many understand this to be an appearance of the pre-incarnate Christ, the LORD Himself in visible form. This has been the dominant reading in the church since the early centuries.

views.label: The LORD manifest, closely tied to the angel of the LORD
views.case: The scene parallels the angel of the LORD at the burning bush, where the messenger and the LORD are spoken of interchangeably, Exodus 3:2-6; on this reading the Commander is the visible manifestation of the LORD, whether or not one specifies the Son, and the point is that God Himself has come to lead the war.

views.label: Michael, the great prince over Israel
views.case: Daniel calls Michael one of the chief princes and the great prince who stands watch over God's people, Daniel 10:13,21 and 12:1, using the same rank Joshua's Commander bears; on this reading the figure is a mighty created angel who leads Israel's cause in the unseen realm, distinct from the LORD Himself, and worship language in verse 14 is read as respectful homage rather than proof of deity.

debates.bearing: Genesis keeps the spotlight on the human choice and on God's verdict, and it never lets the tempter excuse the tempted. What decides the question here is that the Commander does not refuse worship as Michael's fellow angel later does in Revelation 22:8-9, and He personally consecrates the ground, a divine prerogative no delegated prince claims elsewhere. That combination pushes the first two readings well ahead of the third, while still leaving the precise identity, whether the LORD Himself or the eternal Son before His birth, a matter the text does not spell out further.

debates.question: Does Joshua's act of falling facedown by itself prove the Commander is divine?

views.label: Prostration was common courtesy, not proof of deity
views.case: Falling facedown was regularly given to human superiors in Israel; David bows facedown before Saul in a cave, 1 Samuel 24:8, and Mephibosheth falls facedown before David, 2 Samuel 9:6. If prostration alone were the test, both scenes would require worshiping a mere king, so the gesture by itself cannot settle who stands before Joshua.

views.label: The declaration of holy ground turns courtesy into worship
views.case: Whatever the bow alone would prove, the Commander does not merely receive it and move on; He goes further and makes the ground itself holy by His presence, exactly the claim reserved for the LORD at the burning bush, Exodus 3:5. No king, however honored, could rightly say that of the dirt beneath his sandals, so it is this claim, not the posture, that seals the case.

debates.bearing: Together the two views show that it is not the bowing alone that reveals who stands before Joshua, since bowing was given to kings every day, but the combination of accepted worship and the claim to holy ground. Either mark alone would be inconclusive; together they leave no room for reading the Commander as merely human.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond the three words already named, several more repay attention. The narrator first calls the figure simply ish, a man, the ordinary Hebrew word for a human male, the same word used of the three visitors Abraham entertains at Mamre, one of whom turns out to be the LORD Himself, Genesis 18:2, and of the mysterious man who wrestles Jacob at the Jabbok until dawn, Genesis 32:24. The vocabulary itself withholds the figure's identity; an Israelite hearing a man before Jericho would have no reason yet to expect anything more than a scout or a foreign officer.

That expectation is reinforced by the title itself. Sar, commander or prince, is not a supernatural word; it is the standard rank given to human generals elsewhere in the historical books, Sisera the commander of Jabin's army, Judges 4:2, and Abner the commander of Saul's army, 2 Samuel 2:8. Joshua's blunt question, are You for us or for our enemies, is exactly what a general asks of a rival officer. The shock is not the title but what follows it, commander of the tsava of the LORD, so that an apparently ordinary rank turns out to belong to the host of heaven itself.

Joshua's response is described in two stages before the single word shachah is reached: he nafal, fell, and did so al panav, upon his face, the standard idiom for full prostration; only then comes shachah, the act of worship proper. Some grammarians note that shachah is built on an unusual verb stem, sometimes labeled the Hishtaphel, a form scarcely used for any other Hebrew root, as though the language itself sets this act of homage apart from ordinary bowing. Joshua's compliance in verse 15 is described with the simple word na'al, sandal, the very item Ruth 4:7 and Deuteronomy 25:9-10 treat as an ordinary object in everyday legal transactions. Here, at God's word, the ordinary sandal becomes the thing that must come off, because the ground beneath it, qodesh, is no longer common ground at all.

The ancient Greek translation of Joshua renders the figure's title with a single compound word, archistrategos, chief general or commander in chief, a term later Christian writers borrowed for the archangel Michael. Joshua's Hebrew never uses that Greek compound, but the translators plainly heard in commander of the tsava of the LORD something more than an ordinary field officer, a supreme commander over every armed rank beneath him. Man, commander, fall, face, sandal: each word starts in the everyday and is lifted, by what follows it, into the presence of God.

typology.type: The Commander who leads the LORD's heavenly army, Joshua 5:14
typology.fulfillment: Joshua's Commander is unnamed and unseen again after this scene, a single, veiled appearance before the first battle. The correspondence sharpens in the New Testament, where Jesus is called the pioneer, or captain, of salvation, made perfect through suffering to bring many sons to glory, Hebrews 2:10, and is seen riding at the head of heaven's armies, robed and crowned, the Word of God, Revelation 19:11-14. Where the Commander at Jericho stayed hidden after one meeting, Christ's captaincy is now revealed fully and permanently; the type is a single glimpse, and the fulfillment is the ongoing reign of the risen Lord over every power in heaven and on earth.

typology.type: Holy ground and the removed sandals, Joshua 5:15
typology.fulfillment: The command matches Moses' own call word for word, take off your sandals, tying Joshua's commission to the same holy presence that sent Moses, Exodus 3:5, a link Stephen repeats when retelling the burning bush before the Sanhedrin, Acts 7:32-33. Both leaders learn that access to God's presence requires reverence, not achievement. In Christ that access is not merely marked by a removed sandal but permanently opened; believers now draw near with confidence, Hebrews 4:16, because the holiness that once demanded distance has itself come near in the incarnate Son. The type shows access guarded; the fulfillment shows access granted for good.

typology.type: The drawn sword of the LORD's Commander, Joshua 5:13
typology.fulfillment: A sword in hand, ready but not yet used, describes a coming battle rather than one already underway; Jericho's fall in the very next chapter is the sword's first stroke. John pictures the ultimate use of that sword in the mouth of the returning Christ, who will strike down the nations and rule them with an iron scepter, Revelation 19:15, and tread the winepress of the wrath of God Almighty. The type falls short only in scale: one city fell to a drawn sword at Jericho, but the whole rebellion of the nations falls at the last to the sword that proceeds from the risen Commander's own mouth.

Joshua assumes the armed stranger must be enlisted for one side or the other, exactly the mistake Peter makes in Gethsemane when he draws a sword to defend Jesus. Jesus corrects him precisely as the Commander corrects Joshua: He does not need Peter's blade, for He could at once call on more than twelve legions of angels, Matthew 26:52-54. Both scenes strip away the assumption that God's cause depends on human weapons or human timing. Where Joshua learns to lay down his question and take orders, Peter is told to put his sword away and let the greater purpose stand, the same lesson taught twice, centuries apart, to two impulsive leaders at the brink of decisive events.

study.christ:
The New Testament never repeats this scene outright, yet its shape recurs at the hinge of the gospel story. In Gethsemane, on the eve of a far greater battle, Peter draws a sword to defend his Lord, exactly the instinct Joshua shows before Jericho, treating the coming conflict as a cause needing a defender. Jesus answers as the Commander answers Joshua: Peter's sword is put away, because if force were the point, more than twelve legions of angels stand ready at a word, Matthew 26:52-54. In both scenes the lesson is the same, God does not need to be armed by human hands; He commands, He does not enlist.

The title itself becomes messianic elsewhere in Scripture. Isaiah promises that God will make His servant a leader and commander of the peoples, Isaiah 55:4, using the language of command for the one who saves. The church has long read Jericho's Commander back into this line, seeing in the drawn sword and the accepted worship a preview of the Son who would one day stand revealed as exactly that, king and commander, no longer veiled in a single wordless scene but named, crucified, and raised.

Revelation completes the picture most explicitly. There the rider called Faithful and True leads the armies of heaven, robed, crowned, with a sword from His mouth to strike the nations, Revelation 19:11-16, the very army whose commander met Joshua outside Jericho now shown in full, at the head of a host dressed in fine linen. Hebrews adds the pastoral note behind the military one: this Commander is also the pioneer of salvation, made perfect through what He suffered so that many sons could be brought to glory, Hebrews 2:10. He does not station Himself over the battle from a safe distance; He goes ahead of His people into it, and bears its cost Himself.

Paul draws the two threads together for the ordinary believer. Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities and made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them in the cross, Colossians 2:15, and He promises that the God of peace will soon crush Satan under the feet of every believer, Romans 16:20, language that borrows the ancient picture of an enemy trampled underfoot. The soldier who once fell facedown before an unnamed Commander outside Jericho was, in the end, kneeling before the very Christ who would win every war that matters by dying rather than by drawing a blade.
study.god:
This scene answers a question every soldier eventually asks under pressure: is God on my side? Joshua puts it plainly, are You for us or for our enemies, and the Commander's flat no reframes the whole relationship. God is not a resource to be allocated to a cause, however good the cause; He is the reality every cause must answer to. The same corrective runs through Israel's later history. When Aram's officers concluded that Israel's God was merely a god of the hills, weaker in the valleys, the LORD deliberately proved otherwise by giving Aram's army into Israel's hand on the plain, 1 Kings 20:23-28, refusing to be filed away as a local or partisan deity, exactly as He refuses Joshua's either-or.

He is also, in this scene, the God who commands armies no human eye can number. The Psalm asks who is this King of glory, and answers that it is the LORD of Hosts, mighty in battle, Psalm 24:8-10, the same title Joshua meets embodied before Jericho. That He appears with a single drawn sword rather than a visible host is itself a statement: the LORD needs no display to make His authority felt, and the size of the force behind Him is never in question.

His holiness is inseparable from His command. He does not simply lead an army; He turns the very dust under Joshua's feet into holy ground by standing on it, exactly as He had done for Moses. Holiness here is relational rather than architectural, belonging to whatever ground God occupies, which means His people carry the weight of that holiness with them wherever He goes ahead of them, a truth that will matter again within two chapters when a hidden theft turns God's own camp into something requiring purging, Joshua 7.

Above all, this is a God who asks for worship before He gives out orders. Joshua's own question, what does my Lord have to say to His servant, models the right order: adoration first, instruction second. A God who must be persuaded to help is not the God of Joshua 5; the God who is met there simply says, take off your sandals, and expects to be obeyed.

crossReferences.note: Moses meets an angel of the LORD in a blazing bush and is told to remove his sandals because the ground is holy, the same command Joshua receives almost word for word. The repetition binds Joshua's ministry to Moses' and signals that the same LORD who called Moses at Horeb now personally opens Joshua's first campaign.

Balaam's eyes are opened to see the angel of the LORD standing in the road with a drawn sword, and he too falls facedown. A drawn sword and a facedown response appear three times in the historical books, with Balaam, with David, and with Joshua, showing this was a recognizable form of encounter with the LORD's messenger, not an isolated device.

David looks up and sees the angel of the LORD standing between heaven and earth with a drawn sword stretched out over Jerusalem, and he and the elders fall facedown in sackcloth. Unlike Joshua's encounter, this sword threatens judgment on Israel itself, showing the same armed figure who fights for God's people can also stand against them when they sin.

Stephen retells the burning bush before the Sanhedrin, quoting the LORD's own words, take off your sandals, almost exactly as Joshua hears them. His sermon uses Moses' commissioning to argue that the God who met Moses on holy ground had already been rejected once by Israel's ancestors, a warning Stephen presses on hearers who are, in that moment, rejecting Him again.

God promises to make His servant a witness to the nations, a leader and commander of the peoples. The prophecy takes the ordinary word for a ruler and applies it to the coming Servant, giving the language of command a messianic future the unnamed Commander at Jericho only foreshadows.

The rider called Faithful and True leads the armies of heaven and strikes the nations with a sword from His mouth. This is the fullest unveiling of the figure Joshua meets in shadow, the Commander no longer glimpsed once outside a single city but revealed permanently at the head of every rank of heaven.

Jesus is called the pioneer, or captain, of salvation, made perfect through suffering to bring many sons to glory. The military title given to the Commander at Jericho becomes, in Christ, a title bound up with suffering rather than command alone, since He leads His people into glory by going through death first.

When John falls to worship the angel who has shown him the visions of Revelation, the angel refuses at once, insisting he is only a fellow servant and pointing John back to God. The refusal is the exact opposite of what happens at Jericho, where the Commander accepts Joshua's worship without correction, marking Him as more than any created angel.

In Gethsemane Peter draws a sword to defend Jesus, assuming the cause needs his blade, and Jesus tells him to put it away, since He could at once call on more than twelve legions of angels. The scene answers the same mistaken instinct Joshua shows before Jericho, that God's purposes depend on being armed and defended by human hands.

Isaiah sees the LORD of Hosts high and exalted, and his response is not command but collapse, woe is me, for I am ruined. The same divine holiness that sends Isaiah to his knees is the holiness that makes the ground holy under Joshua's feet, a reminder that nearness to this God always undoes human confidence before it commissions anything new.

study.oneStory:
Genesis already promised that a woman's offspring would crush the serpent's head, Genesis 3:15, the first announcement that the great contest running through history is a war, not a negotiation. Every battle in Joshua flows from that older promise, and this small scene outside Jericho is the moment the war's true shape gets named out loud: it belongs to the LORD, and it was never Israel's to wage alone. Israel had already left slavery in Egypt through a war it did not fight, the LORD will fight for you, Exodus 14:14, so this is not a new idea, only its clearest statement yet, on the very ground where the conquest is about to begin in earnest.

From here the pattern repeats across the rest of the Old Testament. Gideon is told to trim his army until victory can only be credited to the LORD, Judges 7. David refuses Saul's armor and fights with a sling, so that the battle is the LORD's, 1 Samuel 17:47. Each episode is this same encounter told again in a different key: God's people prevail only when they stop treating God as their weapon and start taking their place under His command.

The New Testament brings the pattern to its center. Christ is revealed as the Commander this scene only glimpses, no longer bearing a drawn sword in a single field but leading the full armies of heaven, Revelation 19:11-16, and He wins the decisive victory not by human strength but by His own death and resurrection, disarming every hostile power, Colossians 2:15. His people now fight, if the word still applies, with weapons that are not of the flesh, 2 Corinthians 10:4, waiting for the day every remaining enemy is placed under His feet, 1 Corinthians 15:25. The scene before Jericho is a small window onto that entire story, one army commanded by one Lord, moving from Eden's first promise to the last battle in Revelation, where the outcome was decided before Joshua ever fell facedown in the dust.

quiz.q: How did the Commander answer Joshua's question, are You for us or for our enemies?

options.text: Neither; He had come as Commander of the LORD's army to lead, not to take a side.
options.note: Verse 14 reframes the whole encounter: God comes to command, not to be recruited.

options.text: He said He was firmly on Israel's side against Jericho.
options.note: Israel would indeed be given the victory, but His answer was Neither; He came to lead His own war, not to join Israel's.

options.text: He refused to answer and vanished.
options.note: He answered clearly and gave Joshua instructions; He did not vanish without a word.

options.text: He said He had come to fight for Jericho.
options.note: He had not come for the enemy; He came as Commander of the LORD's army.

quiz.q: How did Joshua respond to the Commander?

options.text: He fell facedown in worship and asked for the Commander's orders.
options.note: Verse 14 shows Joshua worshiping and submitting, the fitting response to the divine Commander.

options.text: He saluted Him as a fellow officer and shook His hand.
options.note: He treated Him not as an equal but as Lord, falling facedown before Him.

options.text: He drew his own sword to test the stranger.
options.note: He did approach and challenge Him at first, but on hearing the answer he fell down in worship, he did not fight.

options.text: He ran back to camp in fear.
options.note: He did not flee; he bowed in reverence and asked for orders.

quiz.q: What command did the Commander give Joshua, and why?

options.text: To take off his sandals, because the place where he stood was holy.
options.note: Verse 15 echoes Moses at the burning bush; the ground is holy because the LORD is present.

options.text: To sharpen his weapons for the battle ahead.
options.note: Battle was coming, but the command here was to remove his sandals on holy ground, not to prepare weapons.

options.text: To build an altar on the spot at once.
options.note: No altar is commanded here; Joshua is told to remove his sandals because the ground is holy.

options.text: To gather the elders for a council of war.
options.note: The command was personal reverence before the holy God, not a council.

quiz.q: What does this encounter reveal about the conquest?

options.text: It is the LORD's war, led by His Commander, into which Israel is summoned, not merely Israel's war that God assists.
options.note: The answer Neither and the demand for worship reframe the whole campaign as God's.

options.text: It is a war Israel must win by its own strategy and strength.
options.note: Israel fights, but the scene stresses that the war and the command belong to the LORD, not to human strategy.

options.text: It is an ordinary military campaign with no divine involvement.
options.note: The opposite: the divine Commander Himself appears to lead it.

options.text: It shows that God had abandoned Israel to face Jericho alone.
options.note: God had come as Commander to lead them; He had not abandoned them.

questions: Joshua asked whose side God was on, and God reframed the question. Where might you be asking God to bless your plans rather than surrendering to His?
The Commander came to be worshiped and obeyed, not recruited. What would change in your prayers if you approached God more as Commander than as helper?
The ground became holy simply because the LORD was present. How does an awareness of God's holy presence change the way you carry yourself in ordinary places?
Joshua fell facedown and asked, what does my Lord have to say to His servant? Is that your posture before God, ready to receive orders rather than give them?
The true Captain of the LORD's hosts is Christ, who wins the decisive battle. How does knowing that the outcome rests on Him rather than on you steady you in your struggles this week?

translationNotes.note: Fell facedown in reverence renders shachah, which the BSB footnote also gives as paid homage or worshiped; the Commander receives this worship, marking Him as more than a creature.
Commander of the LORD's army translates a title tied to the frequent name the LORD of hosts, the God who leads the armies of heaven.
The command to remove the sandals on holy ground deliberately echoes Exodus 3:5, binding Joshua's encounter to Moses' call at the burning bush.
